diagnosis.primary_pattern: Wind-Cold Constraining the Exterior with Qi-Blood Insufficiency
diagnosis.pathomechanism: COVID-19 infection severely depleted the patient's Defensive Qi (Wei Qi) and consumed Yin fluids during acute illness. During the weakened recovery phase 5 days post-infection, an acute Wind-Cold pathogenic factor invaded the Taiyang (Bladder) and Shaoyang (Gallbladder) meridians, particularly affecting the facial nerves along the Gallbladder pathway. The underlying Qi-Blood insufficiency prevents proper nourishment of the meridians and activation of facial musculature. The pale tongue indicates Qi-Blood deficiency; the white coating represents the body's inability to transform fluids in the presence of pathogen. The floating, tense pulse confirms acute exterior pathogen with meridian tension and pain. This combination results in facial nerve paralysis with numbness (meridians not nourished by Blood), facial drooping (Qi too weak to lift), and ear pain (Gallbladder meridian pathway affected).
diagnosis.disease_cause: Viral infection (COVID-19) depleting systemic Qi and Wei Qi → Weakened immune and meridian defensive function → Secondary acute Wind-Cold pathogen invasion during recovery phase → Meridian obstruction and Qi-Blood insufficiency preventing facial nerve function

constitution.type: Qi-Deficient Constitution (temporarily acute, reactive to viral infection)
constitution.characteristics: Post-viral exhaustion, pale complexion, weak voice and energy, susceptibility to pathogen invasion, impaired body defense mechanisms. Pale tongue with white coating indicates Spleen Qi dysfunction and inability to defend against exterior pathogens.
constitution.tendencies: Prone to exterior pathogen invasions (colds, flu, acute meridian disorders); slow recovery from viral infections; meridian disorders including Bell's palsy, facial nerve paralysis, and other cranial nerve involvement when exposed to wind during recovery phase
constitution.percentage_match: Very strong match (85%+) — recent COVID-19 created acute Qi deficiency state; constitutional weakness predisposed patient to Wind-Cold invasion during recovery

analysis.summary:
This 23-year-old male presents with acute right-sided facial paralysis (House-Brackmann grade IV) five days following COVID-19 infection, accompanied by facial numbness, facial asymmetry, and right ear pain. The clinical presentation is consistent with Bell's palsy (peripheral 7th cranial nerve paralysis) in the acute post-viral phase.

From the inquiry, the key finding is the tight temporal relationship to COVID-19 (5 days ago), placing this clearly in the acute recovery phase when the body is maximally immunocompromised. The specific combination of numbness (meridian malnourishment), facial droop (Qi weakness), and ear pain (Gallbladder meridian involvement) points to Wind-Cold pathogen invasion of the facial meridians during this vulnerable period.

The pale tongue with white fur is diagnostic: the pale color indicates Qi-Blood insufficiency from the viral infection; the white coating indicates the body's inability to expel pathogenic factors (either retained Wind-Cold or impaired fluid transformation from Spleen Yang weakness). The floating, tense pulse directly confirms acute exterior Wind-Cold pathogen (floating = exterior, tense = cold/pain/meridian obstruction). These signs are fully compatible with an acute exterior pattern overlaid on chronic Qi deficiency.

The primary pattern is Wind-Cold Constraining the Exterior complicated by significant underlying Qi-Blood insufficiency. This is NOT a pure deficiency pattern (the floating, tense pulse and acute 5-day onset rule that out), nor a heat pattern (pale tongue, white coat, and post-viral context contradict heat). This is a mixed (excess-deficiency) presentation requiring dual strategy: expel the Wind-Cold pathogen while simultaneously tonifying Qi-Blood to restore meridian nourishment and facial nerve function.

Prognostically, House-Brackmann grade IV (approximately 50% facial function) is moderately severe but not complete paralysis (grade VI). With appropriate early intervention in TCM, significant recovery is expected within 2-4 weeks. The key is distinguishing the viral post-acute state from a purely deficient presentation—the exterior pathogenic component must be expelled, not merely tonified.

key_findings.from_inquiry: Acute onset (5 days post-COVID-19) peripheral facial paralysis with numbness and asymmetry; ear pain present; House-Brackmann grade IV indicates 50% function loss; timing during recovery phase indicates immune/Qi vulnerability; no mention of fever, headache severity, or prior herpes simplex exposure (but Bell's palsy may be post-viral rather than herpetic)
key_findings.from_visual: Pale tongue body indicates Qi-Blood insufficiency from viral exhaustion; white coating indicates exterior pathogen/fluid transformation failure; inability to assess facial appearance directly but paralysis and asymmetry noted; pale color throughout suggests systemic rather than local heat
key_findings.from_pulse: Floating quality confirms acute exterior pathogenic invasion (not deep/constitutional deficiency); tense/tight quality indicates cold nature of pathogen and meridian pain/obstruction; together floating-tense is classic for Wind-Cold exterior, particularly appropriate for facial paralysis onset
key_findings.from_other: Post-viral timing is critical diagnostic clue—Bell's palsy has higher incidence in viral recovery phases when immune function is lowest; age 23 (relatively young) favors good prognosis; no history of previous facial paralysis or prior Bell's palsy mentioned

analysis.pattern_rationale: Wind-Cold Constraining the Exterior with Qi-Blood Insufficiency is identified as follows: (1) Floating, tense pulse = exterior Wind-Cold confirmed; (2) Pale tongue = Qi-Blood deficiency from COVID-19; (3) White coating = exterior cold pathogen present / Spleen Yang unable to transform fluids; (4) Acute 5-day onset post-viral = exterior pattern timing; (5) Facial paralysis = Qi too weak to activate meridians, Blood too deficient to nourish them; (6) Numbness = meridian malnourishment despite qi obstruction; (7) Ear pain = Gallbladder meridian (Shaoyang) pathway involvement, consistent with Wind-Cold invasion of facial routes. Secondary patterns included because: Gallbladder meridian obstruction is evidenced by ear pain and facial drooping (Gallbladder governs the side of the head/ear); Spleen Yang deficiency is inferred from pale tongue, white coat, and post-viral Qi exhaustion. This pattern is NOT Liver Qi Stagnation (no emotional/chest symptoms), NOT Central Bell's palsy (acute peripheral presentation), NOT pure Qi deficiency (floating pulse and acute exterior signs present)—it is correctly classified as acute exterior with deficiency complication.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Expel Wind-Cold pathogen from the Exterior while simultaneously tonifying Qi-Blood to nourish the meridians, restore facial nerve function, and strengthen the body's defense against pathogen recurrence. The exterior pathogenic component is addressed first (to release constraint), then Qi-Blood tonification follows to enable meridian nourishment and healing.
treatment.treatment_method: Week 1-2: Primary focus on releasing the exterior Wind-Cold using warming, expelling herbs combined with Qi tonification. Week 2-6: Transition to sustained Qi-Blood tonification as acute exterior signs resolve, with continued meridian opening and local facial stimulation. Acupuncture/acupressure should focus on local facial points (Taiyang, Yangbai, Dicang, Yingxiang) combined with distal points (Hegu, Fengchi) and meridian-tonifying points (Zusanli). Do NOT begin needling in first 24-48 hours if acute inflammation is present; massage and herbal therapy take precedence initially.

beneficial: Ginseng (Panax ginseng, Ren Shen) — directly replenishes Defensive Qi and systemic Qi exhausted by COVID-19; warming without excessive heat; essential for post-viral recovery
Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus, Huang Qi) — tonifies Defensive Qi specifically to strengthen exterior resistance; prevents Wind pathogen recurrence; mild warming action
Red Dates (Zizyphus jujuba, Hong Zao) — tonifies both Qi and Blood simultaneously; easily digestible; sweet nature supports Spleen Qi function; can be eaten daily
Chicken (whole bird or breast, Ji Rou) — warming protein source; tonifies Qi more gently than red meat; supports meridian function during recovery
Shiitake or Wood Ear Mushrooms (Hong Gu) — tonify Qi and support immune recovery post-viral; neutral thermal nature so applicable during both acute and recovery phases
recipes: Ginseng-Chicken Strengthening Soup: Ginseng slices 6 grams, whole chicken (cleaned, cut into pieces) 200 grams, red dates 6 pieces (pitted), fresh ginger 2-3 slices, water 1.5 liters. Bring water to boil, add all ingredients, reduce heat to low simmer for 90-120 minutes until chicken is tender. Consume once daily in the morning or early afternoon. Best taken 5-7 days per week for first 3 weeks.

Astragalus Daily Immune Tea: Astragalus root 10 grams, red dates 5 pieces (pitted), fresh ginger 1 small slice, filtered water 600 mL. Boil water, add astragalus and ginger, simmer 20 minutes, add dates, steep additional 10 minutes, strain. Drink warm once or twice daily, morning preferred. Take consistently for 4-6 weeks during recovery phase.

foods_to_avoid: Cold or raw foods (salads, cold drinks, iced beverages, refrigerated fruits) — Cold temperature further damages Spleen Yang, preventing Qi tonification and meridian warming; impairs body's ability to expel Wind pathogen
Cooling/damp-forming fruits (watermelon, mango, banana) — counteract warming therapeutic strategy; damp nature complicates Wind pathogen elimination and slows healing
Dairy products (milk, yogurt, cheese) — create phlegm-damp obstruction in meridians; interfere with healing of facial nerve pathway; impair Qi circulation
lifestyle: Avoid facial exposure to wind and air currents — Wind pathogen is still invasive and acute (5-7 days into onset); fans, air conditioning, open windows, and drafts can significantly worsen facial paralysis by allowing additional Wind entry; keep affected side of face covered with scarf when outdoors or in windy conditions for minimum 2-3 weeks

Use warm water (not hot, not cold) for all face washing and bathing — warm temperature supports meridian relaxation and Qi circulation; never apply ice or cold compresses to face; wash with lukewarm water and pat dry gently without rubbing the paralyzed side

Establish early sleep schedule and prioritize sleep duration — Qi is actively restored and meridians are regenerated during sleep (particularly 10 PM-6 AM); post-viral recovery demands extended sleep; aim for 10-12 hours nightly for first 2-3 weeks, then 8-9 hours minimum. Avoid late nights and computer/phone screen time after 9 PM, as this exhausts remaining Yin fluids

Maintain emotional stability and reduce stress — anxiety about permanent facial changes, anger, or frustration damages Liver Qi and diverts healing resources away from meridian repair; practice mindful acceptance of recovery timeline (2-4 weeks typical for grade IV); avoid mirrors initially if viewing paralysis increases anxiety; inform family/friends that this is acute, treatable, and highly likely to resolve with proper care
acupoints: Hegu (Large Intestine 4, 合谷) — Location: On the dorsum of the hand, in the webbing between thumb and index finger at the highest point of the muscle when thumb and index finger are brought together. Massage technique: Apply firm sustained pressure with thumb, gradually increasing depth over 30 seconds, then release. Perform 20-30 slow circular motions. Repeat 2-3 times daily. Purpose: Opens the Qi channels of upper body and head; enhances circulation to facial meridians; classical point for facial paralysis and upper body activation

Yangbai (Gallbladder 14, 陽白) — Location: On the forehead, 1 cun directly above the midpoint of the eyebrow, in the groove above the supraorbital ridge. Massage technique: Using index or middle finger, apply gentle circular massage in clockwise direction, 20-30 rotations per session. Light to moderate pressure (patient should feel gentle pressure but no sharp pain). Repeat 2-3 times daily. Purpose: Local stimulation of facial nerve branches; specific point for facial asymmetry and eye area paralysis; directly on the affected side

Dicang (Stomach 4, 地倉) — Location: On the face, lateral to the angle of the mouth, approximately at the level where upper and lower lips meet when mouth is slightly open, in the nasolabial fold/groove. Massage technique: Using index finger, apply gentle upward and outward massage (toward temples), 20-30 strokes per direction, light to moderate pressure. Avoid pressing directly into mouth. Repeat 2-3 times daily. Purpose: Direct activation of orbicularis oris and buccinator muscles; stimulates facial nerve branches; improves mouth drooping

Fengchi (Gallbladder 20, 風池) — Location: At the base of the skull, in the hollow/depression between the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, approximately level with the external occipital protuberance. Massage technique: Using both thumbs, apply firm, sustained pressure with slow circular massage, 15-20 circles in each direction (clockwise, then counterclockwise), 1-2 minutes per session. Lean head gently forward to facilitate access. Repeat 2-3 times daily. Purpose: Expels pathogenic Wind from upper body; improves overall Qi circulation to head and facial meridians; addresses both Taiyang (Bladder) and Shaoyang (Gallbladder) channels
exercise: Gentle facial muscle activation exercises — Perform slow, intentional facial movements 3 times daily: (1) Slow smile, hold 3 seconds, release (10 repetitions); (2) Gentle frown, hold 3 seconds, release (10 repetitions); (3) Slow eye blink, 20 repetitions; (4) Cheek puff on unaffected side, then attempt on affected side if possible, 10 repetitions; (5) Gentle 'O' mouth shape, hold 3 seconds, 10 repetitions. Perform movements slowly and mindfully, focusing on the facial muscles rather than speed. Duration: 10-15 minutes per session. This retrains neural pathways and prevents muscle atrophy during recovery.

Tai Chi or gentle Qigong — Practice 15-20 minutes daily; promotes whole-body Qi circulation and meridian opening; enhances Defensive Qi function; reduces stress and supports emotional stability during recovery. Specific emphasis on movements that involve the head and neck (gentle neck rotations in Tai Chi, breathing practices that extend to crown in Qigong). Can begin after first 3-5 days once acute inflammation is stabilized.
recommendations.emotional_care: Bell's palsy causes significant emotional distress due to visible facial asymmetry and fear of permanent disfigurement. Patient should understand that Grade IV paralysis is moderately severe but NOT complete loss of function, and recovery potential is high (60-80% full recovery typical with early treatment). Reassurance that this condition is post-viral (not degenerative or permanent), time-limited (typically 2-4 weeks for major improvement), and highly responsive to TCM treatment is essential. Recommend initially avoiding mirrors to reduce anxiety; reintroduce mirror viewing only after visible improvement occurs (typically 5-7 days). Encourage patient to explain the condition to close contacts so they understand the temporary nature and do not assume permanent disability. Maintain hopeful but realistic outlook: recovery will occur but patience is required; stress and anxiety impede healing by disrupting Qi circulation, so emotional regulation is literally therapeutic.

herbal_formulas.name: Astragalus and Ledebouriella Decoction for Wind-Cold Facial Paralysis
herbal_formulas.dosage: Combine all ingredients. Add water to fill pot 1 finger-width above herbs. Bring to boil over high heat, then reduce to low simmer for 40-50 minutes until liquid reduces by half. Strain. Drink 1 cup twice daily (morning and evening), between meals if possible. Continue for 2-3 weeks, then reassess.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This classical formula is specifically indicated for Bell's palsy and acute facial paralysis following viral infection. Ledebouriella expels Wind-Cold pathogen from the Exterior and facial meridians; Astragalus tonifies Qi and Defensive Qi simultaneously while maintaining the formula's warming, expelling nature. Ginger warms the meridians and facilitates herb absorption; dates support overall Qi tonification. This is the first-line herbal formula for the acute (0-3 week) phase of this condition.

herbal_formulas.name: Qi-Tonifying Decoction with Meridian Opening Modification (Modified Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang variant)
ingredients: Ligusticum wallichii (Chuan Xiong) 6 grams (added for facial circulation)
Salvia miltiorrhiza (Dan Shen) 9 grams (added for blood circulation to face)
herbal_formulas.dosage: Combine all ingredients. Prepare as decoction: add water to fill pot 1 finger-width above herbs, bring to boil, reduce to low simmer for 50-60 minutes until liquid reduces by half. Strain. Divide into 2 portions and consume morning and evening, between meals. Use for weeks 3-6 of recovery as the acute exterior phase resolves and the focus shifts to sustained Qi-Blood tonification and facial nerve regeneration.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This is a modified version of the classical Astragalus Qi-Tonifying Decoction, adjusted with added Ligusticum and Salvia to enhance circulation to facial meridians and facial nerve pathways. Used in the later recovery phase (after week 2-3) once acute Wind-Cold signs have largely resolved. Maintains Qi-Blood tonification while opening meridians for sustained facial nerve recovery. Prepare 1 formula at a time; expect slow improvement from week 3-6 with continued treatment.

warning_signs: Rapid worsening of facial paralysis (progression from House-Brackmann IV toward V or VI) within 24-48 hours — suggests more aggressive nerve involvement or secondary inflammation; requires immediate conventional neurological evaluation and imaging (EMG, possibly MRI)

Inability to close the affected eye or development of corneal dryness/irritation — risk of corneal ulcer and permanent vision damage; requires immediate ophthalmological evaluation and protective eye care (lubricating drops, protective tape, eye patch during sleep)
New onset of drooping mouth with severe speech difficulty or drooling — may indicate extension of paralysis beyond 7th cranial nerve; rule out additional CNS involvement
High fever (temperature above 38.5°C / 101.3°F) combined with facial paralysis — raises concern for meningitis, encephalitis, or other serious CNS infection; requires emergency hospital evaluation

Hearing loss, vertigo, or balance problems appearing alongside facial paralysis — suggests Ramsey Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus, related but different from simple Bell's palsy); requires antiviral medication and specialized treatment
Severe ear pain with discharge or visible rash in ear canal — may indicate herpes zoster oticus or secondary infection; requires immediate medical evaluation
contraindications: Do NOT attempt acupuncture (needle insertion) on a severely Qi-deficient patient without qualified, licensed acupuncturist supervision — improper needle technique or excessive needling in the acute phase can cause Qi collapse and worsen paralysis; acupressure (massage) is safer in the first 48-72 hours

Avoid aggressive facial massage or stretching in the first 3-5 days if facial swelling or inflammation is present — overstimulation can trigger spasticity and muscle tightening rather than relaxation; gentle massage only until acute inflammation subsides

Do NOT apply heat packs or moxibustion directly to the face if there is any visible redness, swelling, or inflammation — excessive heat in acute inflammatory phase can worsen facial nerve damage; wait until inflammation visibly decreases

Avoid acupuncture on certain points (such as needling deeply at Dicang or Yangbai) if patient has difficulty closing the eye or significant swelling — risk of needle trauma to delicate facial structures; use acupressure instead
precautions.special_notes: This patient's condition is Bell's palsy (idiopathic peripheral 7th cranial nerve paralysis), most likely post-viral given temporal relationship to COVID-19. While TCM treatment is highly indicated and can accelerate recovery, the patient should be aware that conventional medicine may recommend oral corticosteroids (Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily for 5-7 days, then taper) and possibly antivirals (Valacyclovir) if HSV reactivation is suspected — these can be used concurrently with TCM treatment and often improve outcomes when initiated early (within 72 hours of onset). This patient is now 5 days post-onset, so if not already on steroids, the window is closing but not closed. TCM should be initiated immediately regardless, as it complements conventional treatment and enhances both healing speed and quality of recovery. House-Brackmann grade IV carries prognosis of approximately 50% immediate function and 70-80% eventual complete recovery with treatment; without treatment, spontaneous recovery occurs in only 40-50% of cases. Early intervention is critical. Monitor for synkinesis (involuntary facial movement during voluntary movement) during recovery — this is normal and usually self-resolves within 3-6 months post-onset. If facial paralysis fails to improve by 50% within 2-3 weeks, or worsens, escalate to conventional neurological imaging and evaluation to rule out other causes (Lyme disease, temporal bone fracture, parotid pathology, CNS tumors). Drug-herb interaction note: If patient is prescribed Prednisone, mild warming tonics (Ginseng, Astragalus) are compatible and actually supportive; if Valacyclovir or other antivirals are prescribed, no significant interactions with the recommended herbal formulas. If patient is on any blood-thinning medications, Dan Shen (Salvia) should be avoided or monitored.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess patient status at 2 weeks from treatment start (approximately 7 days from initial symptom onset). Primary markers: reduction in facial numbness, improvement in ability to voluntarily move affected facial muscles (smile, blink, cheek movement), reduction in ear pain. Tongue and pulse should be rechecked; white coating should begin to diminish if exterior pathogen is being expelled; pulse should remain floating but become less tense.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1-2: Ear pain should significantly improve or resolve; numbness should begin to decrease; patient may notice slight voluntary movement returning to affected side (especially if attempting facial exercises). Tongue coating may still be present but should appear less thick. Week 2-3: Visible improvement in smile symmetry and eye closure; facial drooping should be less pronounced (House-Brackmann may improve from IV toward III); numbness essentially resolved. By week 4: Approximately 50-70% normal facial function restored. Complete recovery (95-100%) typically occurs within 6-8 weeks with continued treatment.
follow_up.next_steps: If improvement is evident at 2-week reassessment: Continue present herbal formula through week 3, then transition to the modified Qi-tonifying formula (Bu Zhong Yi Qi Tang variant) for weeks 4-6. Maintain daily acupoint massage and facial exercises indefinitely until complete recovery. Begin professional acupuncture 2-3 times per week if not already doing so, as needling offers superior outcomes to self-massage alone in weeks 2-4 of recovery. If minimal or no improvement at 2-week mark: (1) Verify patient compliance with herbal formula and dietary recommendations; (2) Rule out secondary causes (Lyme disease, temporal bone fracture, parotid involvement) with conventional neurological imaging; (3) Escalate to combination with conventional steroids if not already initiated; (4) Consider referral to specialist acupuncturist experienced in Bell's palsy; (5) Possibly adjust herbal formula if tongue/pulse findings suggest different pattern (e.g. if swelling increases, suggest more emphasis on fluid transformation). Long-term follow-up: After complete recovery, continue occasional ginseng-astragalus tonification (1-2 times per week) for 1-2 months to prevent recurrence and rebuild depleted Qi reserves. Monitor for incomplete recovery or synkinesis; most minor synkinesis self-resolves but severe cases may require continued treatment. Return to normal exercise and exposure (wind exposure, excessive heat/cold) only after facial function is 90%+ normal.

parsed.disclaimer: This Traditional Chinese Medicine diagnosis and treatment recommendations are intended as complementary care and should NOT replace conventional medical evaluation and treatment. Please consult a licensed medical doctor or neurologist for formal diagnosis, imaging studies (MRI, EMG), and conventional treatment options (corticosteroids, antivirals) which may significantly improve outcomes when initiated early. TCM treatment works best when combined with appropriate conventional medical care. This remote TCM assessment is based on limited examination data (no physical palpation, no detailed facial assessment, no complete pulse reading). A licensed TCM practitioner should perform in-person diagnosis and treatment. All herbal formulas should be dispensed and monitored by a qualified herbalist or TCM practitioner. Acupuncture and moxibustion should be administered only by licensed acupuncturists in the patient's jurisdiction. If any warning signs listed above develop, seek immediate conventional medical attention. Recovery timeline and prognosis are estimates based on typical Bell's palsy presentations; individual results may vary.

data.wen_inquiry: Chief complaint: Right-sided facial numbness, asymmetry and ear pain for five days after COVID-19 (House-Brackmann grade IV facial palsy). Symptoms: numbness of the right face; facial droop; ear pain on the right side.
